newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade TV station names new bosses.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade TV station names new bosses.

text.p: Belgrade's Studio B television appointed new bosses nominated by opposition parties, days after the opposition took control of the city council following a three-month battle with the government which dominates most Serbian broadcasting.

The station named its new director and editor-in-chief late on Monday. The president of its new management board, installed straight after the Zajedno (Together) coalition moved into city hall on Friday, said Studio B would not become a mere opposition mouthpiece.

After waging a campaign of mass street protests to get President Slobodan Milosevic to recognise their victories in local elections, Zajedno's leaders promised their next fight would be to free up the country's media, a goal crucial to their chances of beating the ruling Socialists in parliamentary and presidential elections later this year.
Milan Bozic, president of the Studio B managing board, told reporters: "The managing board will not influence its editorial policy".
"Electing a new director and editor-in-chief is the first step towards returning Studio B to Belgraders," he added.
The new director Zoran Ostojic was proposed by the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), one of Zajedno's three member parties.
SPO leader Vuk Draskovic said in a statement he expected Studio B to become a symbol of the journalism "which cannot be bought or seduced by any political party".
Lila Radonjic, the station's new editor-in-chief, was proposed by the Democratic Party whose leader Zoran Djindjic became mayor of Belgrade last week.

She said the station's policy would be less political than before, when Studio B was under the influence of Socialists who controlled the city council. She said she wanted the board to be composed of all parties represented on the council.
The once-independent station was taken over by the city assembly in 1996. Radonjic asked the board to reinstate all former employees who left then for political reasons.
Bozic said the board would propose Belgrade council add two new members to the board -- one each from Milosevic's Socialists and the hardline nationalist Radical Party.

In a sign the Serbian government might be ready to loosen its grip on the media, new Information Minister Radmila Milentijevic said in Washington on Monday Milosevic would allow opposition politicians access to state-controlled television and radio for elections set for later this year.
She said the government was "in the process of reform...we want to find the most liberal law that governs the press in Western Europe and use it to model our regulations".
The newly-appointed loyalist to Milosevic however warned foreign journalists a week ago over their reporting of opposition protests.

"We must especially hold (foreign journalists) responsible for what they write. This means that if they write something which is not factually correct, we should react and demand that the untruth be corrected," she told the pro-government daily Politika.
